analysis.one_liner: Taxes electricity sellers' profits above a 15% return and uses the money to ease consumers' power bills.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on June 6, 2001, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have placed an excise tax on electricity sellers, taxed at the portion of their profit exceeding a 15% pretax rate of return. Electricity made from wind, sun, or water power would have been exempt. The bill stated Congress's intent that the money go to income-tax reductions for consumers, aimed at low-income people and small businesses hurt by high power prices, and to research tax credits for renewable energy. It was introduced by Rep. Jim McDermott during a period of sharply higher electricity prices and never advanced past the committee referral stage.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers facing high electricity prices, especially low-income households and small businesses, would benefit if the tax revenue was used for consumer tax relief as the bill proposed. Renewable energy producers (wind, solar, hydro) would gain a relative advantage because their electricity is exempt from the tax. Taxpayers funding renewable energy research would gain through the proposed research credits.

how_it_helps.text: The bill taxed the profit on each sale of electricity that exceeded a 15% pretax rate of return, targeting only excess returns rather than normal profits, with the seller liable for payment.

It exempted electricity produced from wind, sun, or water power from the tax, and added an anti-avoidance rule so sales to affiliated companies would be taxed as if sold to an unrelated buyer at market price minus transmission costs.

The bill expressed Congress's intent that the revenue be used to reduce income taxes for consumers to moderate the impact of high prices on the poor or small businesses, and to encourage alternative energy development through research tax credits.

analysis.who_pays: Electric generating companies whose profits exceed a 15% pretax return, which would owe the excise tax; some portion could be passed through to electricity prices depending on market conditions.

drawbacks.text: A windfall profits tax on generation can discourage investment in new power plants at exactly the times supply is tightest, and some of the tax could be passed through to the very consumers it aims to help.

The 15% pretax return threshold is an arbitrary line that treats profits just above and just below it very differently, and the renewable exemption (wind, sun, water only) leaves out other low-emission sources like nuclear or geothermal.
The provisions directing revenue to consumer relief and renewable research were only a non-binding 'sense of Congress,' not a legal requirement, so the money could in principle be spent on anything.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers facing high power prices, the potential upside is real: taxing only excess returns and returning the money as targeted tax relief and renewable research would shift costs from households to high-profit generators. The honest costs are that excess-profits taxes can chill investment in generating capacity and that the consumer-relief side was aspirational rather than binding. On balance the bill leaned toward consumers, but it was a broad-brush instrument rather than a carefully targeted one.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim McDermott introduced the bill on June 6, 2001, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
No further action was taken after the referral; the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, and expired at the end of the 107th Congress on January 3, 2003.
The bill drew only two cosponsors, one Independent and one Democrat, in a House controlled by Republicans.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-profit electric generating companies were better off because the tax never advanced; consumers and small businesses got no relief from excess generator profits, and no renewable research credits were created from this bill.

sides.party_line_note: Only three members were attached to the bill (one Democrat sponsor, one Democrat cosponsor, one Independent cosponsor), and no votes or floor action ever occurred, so no partisan split can be measured; the Republican-controlled House took no action on it.

industries.note: The bill would have taxed the portion of their profits exceeding a 15% pretax return on each electricity sale, with anti-avoidance rules for sales to affiliates. The industry's interest in killing the bill ran against consumers who were paying high power prices and funding those excess returns.

Their electricity would be exempt from the windfall tax, giving them a price advantage over fossil-fired generators, and the bill proposed research tax credits for alternative energy. Consumers benefit from both cheaper taxed-exempt renewables and from research aimed at new supply.
